basic_info.name: eSanjeevani (National Telemedicine Service)
basic_info.description: eSanjeevani is India's national, free telemedicine service, built and maintained by the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC, Mohali) under the Ministry of Electronics and IT (MeitY) and implemented by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), with roots in C-DAC's 2002 'Sanjeevani' store-and-forward plus real-time telemedicine system. It runs two modalities: eSanjeevani AB-HWC, a provider-to-provider (doctor-to-doctor) hub-and-spoke service in which a Community Health Officer at an Ayushman Arogya Mandir/PHC facilitates a consultation with a doctor at a district/tertiary hub, and eSanjeevani OPD, a direct patient-to-doctor service. The single most load-bearing fact is its scale: as of 30 July 2026 the government reported over 48.95 crore (about 489.5 million) cumulative teleconsultations across a network of 19,257 hubs and 1,41,341 spokes, supported by about 2.39 lakh (239,000) onboarded providers - making it the largest government-led telemedicine programme in the world. It is integrated with ABDM so that consultations, e-prescriptions and records can be linked to ABHA and interoperable health records, and since 2023 it has carried an AI Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) providing SNOMED-CT-aligned structured symptom capture and differential-diagnosis suggestions to doctors. It is a remote consultation-delivery rail, not a pre-consultation history-capture system: it conducts history during the (remote) visit, requires cloud connectivity, and does not perform in-person OPD intake, paper-document digitization into FHIR, or automated physician-ready summary generation.
basic_info.organization: Developed/operated by the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Mohali (MeitY); implemented by the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW); ABDM integration via the National Health Authority (NHA).

technical_features.what_it_does: eSanjeevani delivers remote outpatient consultations and the associated clinical record. In the AB-HWC (doctor-to-doctor) model a CHO performs an initial assessment at a spoke facility and, when needed, connects the patient to a hub doctor by video; in the OPD (patient-to-doctor) model a citizen registers, completes a short intake form, optionally uploads prior prescriptions/reports, waits in a virtual queue and is seen by a government-registered practitioner. The doctor reviews the inputs, issues an e-prescription, may arrange referrals or follow-up, and the encounter is captured as an electronic health record. eSanjeevani 2.0 (2023) added audio-video stability, past-consultation attachment, prescription preview/synchronisation, point-of-care diagnostic (PoCD) device integration and a mandatory-weighted 'case/EHR completion score' that requires roughly 75% completeness before a case is sent to a doctor. An embedded AI CDSS presents a Physician Assistance Form for structured symptom entry and returns a differential-diagnosis list plus a rule-engine specialist/department recommendation. This is directly relevant to Module C as a national-scale model of structured clinical-data capture and e-prescription, but it does not generate a single physician-ready pre-consultation summary from patient-elicited history plus digitized documents, and does not do in-person OPD intake.
technical_features.architecture: Cloud-based, population-scale telemedicine platform built on open-source tools, deployed in a hub-and-spoke topology. Spokes (Ayushman Arogya Mandirs, PHCs, sub-district/district hospitals) connect to hubs (medical colleges, CHCs, district hospitals); eSanjeevani OPD is a separate direct-to-patient flow. The platform is modelled on MoHFW EHR guidelines, is compatible with IoT/Bluetooth-enabled diagnostic devices, and uses cloud hosting with an agile architecture. eSanjeevani 2.0 integrates cloud computing and AI. The AI CDSS was built from retrospective eSanjeevani 1.0 data (approximately 64 million consultations, from which about 0.22 million SNOMED-CT-aligned records were extracted, yielding ~29,000 unique symptoms refined to 115, later expanded to 300) and combines a knowledge-based symptom repository, expert-validated logic flow and a rule engine for specialist recommendation. A separate AMRIT/common-API integration bridges external EHRs to eSanjeevani via provider authentication (salted SHA-512) and patient registration APIs. Tele-MANAS (national tele-mental health) and a Ministry of Defence OPD variant are built on the same platform.
technical_features.inputs: Patient registration/demographics with ABHA linkage, a short intake form (complaints), optionally uploaded prior prescriptions and reports, clinical information entered by the CHO/doctor, structured symptom data via the CDSS Physician Assistance Form (age, gender, language and multidimensional symptom attributes), vitals and device data from point-of-care/IoT/bluetooth diagnostics, and in the historical/C-DAC telemedicine lineage, ECG waveforms and radiology/pathology images (DICOM/TWAIN).
technical_features.outputs: An e-prescription (the primary clinical output, generated after consultation), an electronic health record for the encounter with a completion score, specialist/department recommendations and differential-diagnosis suggestions for the doctor's use, referral pathways, and ABHA-linked longitudinal health records that can be stored in a patient's chosen health locker and shared with consent. In the ABDM frame these records are intended to circulate as FHIR R4 documents; eSanjeevani does not produce a bespoke summary Composition of its own beyond the prescription/OP record it generates.
technical_features.standards_compliance: Claimed/partially validated: eSanjeevani is officially integrated with ABDM and aligned with ABDM building blocks - ABHA, Healthcare Professionals Registry, Health Facility Registry and interoperable EHR - and both variants completed ABDM integration (announced 2022), so records can be created, linked and shared via ABHA and stored in health lockers. It is modelled on MoHFW EHR guidelines and complies with the NMC Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (2020). The ABDM data-exchange layer is HL7 FHIR R4 with NRCeS India-specific profiles (e.g. PrescriptionRecord, OPConsultRecord, HealthDocumentRecord). The AI CDSS symptom repository is described as SNOMED CT-aligned. Important caveat: the peer-reviewed eSanjeevani utilisation study states the platform did not employ standardised diagnostic coding systems such as ICD-10 or SNOMED CT and that national monitoring could not track patients by ABHA during the study period; and an independent 2026 Intelehealth policy brief explicitly criticises eSanjeevani for not being properly interoperable with ABDM or other national portals. So ABDM/FHIR conformance is officially claimed and partly real, but independently contested and not uniformly implemented.
technical_features.offline_capability: [uncertain / effectively none] eSanjeevani is a cloud-based, real-time telemedicine platform: consultations, records and e-prescriptions depend on network connectivity, and poor broadband in many HWCs is repeatedly cited as a core operational limitation. There is no documented offline-first mode, encrypted local store-and-forward queue or on-device operation for the modern eSanjeevani platform. (Its ancestor, C-DAC's 2002 'Sanjeevani', was explicitly designed as a store-and-forward plus real-time hybrid usable over low-bandwidth links, but that legacy capability is not a documented feature of eSanjeevani 2.0.) Treat current offline capability as absent/unverified.
technical_features.languages_supported: eSanjeevani web application supports 15 languages - English, Hindi, Kannada, Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Assamese, Odia, Bengali, Punjabi, Urdu, Manipuri and Konkani - while the mobile application supports 14 (the same list without Urdu). This is a major contrast with English-first local tools and directly relevant to Module C's bilingual/Hindi requirement. A Bhashini-integrated speech-to-speech translation pilot aims to let patients speak in their own language and have it rendered into the doctor's language on the fly, initially Hindi-English; speech-to-speech/transcription PoCs are being run at C-DAC Mohali but were still not confirmed in production.
technical_features.deployment_model: Cloud-hosted national platform accessed through a web browser and Android/iOS mobile apps; spokes require at least a computer, webcam, microphone and high-resolution scanner plus connectivity. No kiosk or on-premises inference is required; heavy compute is server-side. Hubs are staffed at medical colleges/CHCs/district hospitals, and doctors can consult in shifts. eSanjeevani is also replicated for other programmes (Tele-MANAS mental health, Ministry of Defence national OPD, tele-rehabilitation).

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: The Haryana comparative pilot (57,288 teleconsultations) reported that eSanjeevani 2.0 reduced inadequate case details by 2.23% and consultations with no audio-video connectivity by 8.2%, improving consultation quality by 7.75%, with 65% of participants preferring 2.0; but it also flagged unresolved dashboard optimisation and chief-complaint refinement problems. The AI CDSS study (medRxiv, 2022-2024) reports improved structured data capture and diagnostic precision and streamlined triage, but its published framing is implementation-oriented rather than a controlled diagnostic-accuracy trial - it does not report a sensitivity/specificity/F1 for the differential-diagnosis suggestions. Government figures state that from April 2023 to July 2026 about 30.4 crore consultations benefited from standardised data capture and about 2.13 crore (21.3 million) received AI-based differential diagnoses. No peer-reviewed diagnostic-accuracy figure for the CDSS was located.
performance_metrics.latency: [uncertain] No published latency, throughput or time-to-record metric was found. Operationally, the platform has reported peaks above 128,000 consultations in a single day, but per-consultation latency is not documented.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: [uncertain] Not published as compute specifications, because processing runs in C-DAC's cloud. Spoke-site requirements are documented as endpoint hardware - a computer, webcam, microphone and high-resolution scanner - plus internet bandwidth; the server-side CPU/GPU/RAM footprint is not disclosed. This matters because MediKiosk must run the equivalent of some of this capture on a ~4GB CPU/iGPU kiosk rather than in a cloud.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Cumulative teleconsultations rose steeply: >163M (Sep 2023), >276M (Nov 2024), over 43 crore (23 Nov 2025, Rajya Sabha), 282M consultations benefiting from CDSS (Apr 2023-Nov 2025), >47 crore (Jul 2026, Rajnath Singh), over 48 crore (26 Jul 2026), and 48.95 crore cumulative across all states/UTs as of 30 July 2026. Network as of 30 Jul 2026: 19,257 hubs and 1,41,341 spokes; FY2024-25 alone contributed over 11 crore consultations; ~2,39,281 onboarded providers; 890 online OPDs. The AB-HWC provider-assisted model accounts for more than 93% of usage. More than 57% of beneficiaries are women and about 14% are senior citizens. CDSS: ~30.4 crore consultations benefited from standardised data capture and ~2.13 crore from AI differential diagnoses (Apr 2023-Jul 2026).
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Mixed and largely government-operated. Quality/utilisation evidence comes from (a) peer-reviewed studies - a comparative e-Sanjeevani 2.0 vs 1.0 pilot in Haryana (Health and Technology, 2024) and an adoption/utilisation analysis using C-DAC programme data (Oxford Open Digital Health / PMC, 2025) - and (b) a medRxiv prospective implementation study of the CDSS (2022-2024). Programme volumes and the CDSS adoption counts are official MoHFW/Lok Sabha/PIB figures rather than independent audit. Independent scrutiny exists (Intelehealth policy brief, Sep 2026; IMPRI analysis, Jun 2026) and is critical on quality - target-driven 'ghost consultations', brief/incomplete consultations, weak triage and interoperability gaps. No blinded clinician concordance or concept-recall benchmark of its record/summary quality was found.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: eSanjeevani is the strongest evidence that India's national digital-health rails work at population scale, and it is simultaneously the clearest proof of the exact gap MediKiosk Module C targets. It validates that: (1) ABDM/ABHA-linked interoperable records and e-prescriptions can be operated across all states/UTs; (2) Indians will engage with digital-first care in very large numbers; and (3) government is willing to fund and procure large telemedicine infrastructure. For Module C specifically, eSanjeevani supplies a living reference for the output side - an e-prescription/OP record that must be ABHA-linkable and ABDM/FHIR-oriented - and its CDSS is the closest existing national-scale artefact to structured pre-consultation symptom capture, showing that a SNOMED-CT-aligned structured form can be driven by non-physicians. But it does not solve MediKiosk's core problem: eSanjeevani is remote and during-visit; it does not capture a structured history in person at the OPD door, does not digitize the patient's physical documents into FHIR resources, and does not synthesize history plus documents into one bilingual physician-ready summary. Its CDSS suggests differential diagnoses to a doctor - a different posture from Module C's elicit-never-diagnose, deterministic summary renderer. MediKiosk can therefore position Module C as the missing in-person, document-aware, pre-consultation front end to the same national rail that eSanjeevani already travels on.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) the ABDM/ABHA-native output posture - everything the kiosk captures should be linkable to ABHA and shareable via consent, matching eSanjeevani's integration model; (2) the 'EHR completion score' idea - weighted field completeness that gates a record before it reaches the doctor - as a direct, proven mechanism for raising history quality on a kiosk; (3) multilingual delivery as a first-class requirement (eSanjeevani ships 14-15 Indian languages), validating MediKiosk's bilingual commitment and the Bhashini-style speech-to-speech approach; (4) the deterministic, rule-engine style of the CDSS specialist-recommendation logic, which is CPU-friendly and explainable - though Module C must stop short of diagnosis; (5) PoCD/device and DICOM/TWAIN interoperability patterns for pulling vitals and scanned images into the record. Reject/guard against: (1) cloud dependency and real-time assumptions - eSanjeevani fails precisely where connectivity is weak, whereas Module C is offline-first; (2) target-driven volume metrics that produced 'ghost' and thin consultations - Module C should measure summary completeness and clinician usefulness, not consultation counts; (3) any drift into autonomous diagnosis - the CDSS is doctor-directed decision support, and Module C's elicit-never-diagnose boundary is stricter; (4) reliance on a live national gateway for the kiosk to function; local capture and queued, consent-gated sync are required.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Connectivity: the platform is cloud/real-time, and poor broadband at HWCs is a persistent, officially acknowledged problem - a hard blocker for the offline-first kiosk model, and the reason MediKiosk cannot simply imitate the architecture. Interoperability is contested: while ABDM integration is officially claimed and ABHA linkage is real, an independent 2026 policy brief states eSanjeevani remains poorly interoperable with ABDM and other national portals, causing data re-entry - so 'ABDM-integrated' should be cited cautiously. Diagnostic coding: the peer-reviewed utilisation study notes the platform did not use ICD-10/SNOMED CT for its aggregate diagnostic data, and could not track patients by ABHA during study periods, limiting continuity-of-care claims. Quality: independent analyses document target-driven 'ghost consultations', brief/incomplete encounters, weak triage and transactional rather than holistic care. No public diagnostic-accuracy figure exists for the AI CDSS, and its outputs are doctor-facing suggestions, not validated diagnoses. There is also a gap between government cumulative figures from different dates (43 crore in Nov 2025, 48.95 crore in Jul 2026, 330M+ in an independent brief), so figures must be dated and sourced.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: eSanjeevani and MediKiosk are complementary, not head-to-head. eSanjeevani is a cloud, online, remote-consultation delivery rail operating across the whole country; MediKiosk is an offline-first, patient-facing, in-person OPD kiosk that captures history before the visit and digitizes physical documents. eSanjeevani conducts history during a remote encounter and hands a live doctor an e-prescription; Module C produces one structured, bilingual, physician-ready summary before the consultation, with per-field provenance, physician attestation and NRCeS OPConsultRecord emission. eSanjeevani's scale strengthens rather than erodes MediKiosk's differentiation: it proves the ABDM/ABHA national rail and large-scale public willingness to use digital-first care, while leaving the pre-consultation, offline-capable, document-aware intake and summary layer unbuilt. The one caution is strategic: because eSanjeevani already owns the national telemedicine rail and ABDM integration, MediKiosk should integrate with it (e.g. push the summary/prescription into the same ABHA-linked record) rather than compete for remote-consultation volume.

business_info.license: [uncertain] eSanjeevani is a Government of India programme; its source code is not released under an open-source license. It is described as built with open-source tools internally, and the historic Sanjeevani technology was C-DAC proprietary. No public repository or license was found.
business_info.pricing: Free to patients. The service is publicly funded; there is no user fee for consultations. For institutions, deployment may involve state/department funding and may carry costs for third-party components (video conferencing, SMS gateway, cloud hosting, licences) billed as per usage.
business_info.funding: Government-funded through the National Health Mission and the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission. Under ABDM, the Union Budget 2024-25 allocated Rs 200 crore to digital health infrastructure; the Union health budget grew cumulatively ~194% over 12 years (per the Defence Minister, July 2026). No private funding - it is a public programme.
business_info.commercial_status: Government programme / public digital infrastructure, delivered as a free national service rather than a commercial product.

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Primarily the private Indian telemedicine and digital-health apps - Practo, Apollo 24|7, Tata 1mg, MediBuddy, and state/health-system helplines (e.g. Karnataka's earlier Aptamitra) - plus government disease-programme portals it is meant to interoperate with (NCD portal, Nikshay, AB-HWC HMIS). Within Module C's specific space (offline + ABDM + pre-consultation summary), eSanjeevani is not a competitor but a rail; the more direct overlaps are Eka Care (patient-side ABDM PHR/digitization) and offline ABDM entrants such as CureNet.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: ABDM building blocks - ABHA creation/linkage, Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR), Health Facility Registry (HFR), and ABDM health-record exchange (HIP/HIU roles) to allow creation, linking and consent-based sharing of records and storage in health lockers. Point-of-care/IoT and Bluetooth diagnostic devices are integrated (eSanjeevani 2.0), with published work on ATOM 12-lead ECG transmission into eSanjeevani and DICOM/TWAIN imaging modules in the C-DAC telemedicine lineage. Third-party AMRIT/common-API bridges external EHRs to eSanjeevani (provider auth plus patient registration). Bhashini provides speech translation. The same platform underpins Tele-MANAS and a Ministry of Defence national OPD.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: eSanjeevani is a core pillar of Ayushman Bharat and the ABDM, so it sits at the centre of India's public digital-health procurement and standards tailwinds: ABDM-compliant HMIS guidance, NRCeS FHIR R4 profiles, ABHA adoption and National Telemedicine Practice Guidelines (2020). The ecosystem is pushing every serious health-record product toward ABDM/FHIR conformance, which favours MediKiosk's OPConsultRecord emission strategy. At the same time, official reviews show the limits of a volume-first public platform - weak triage, incomplete records, and interoperability gaps - leaving room for higher-quality, capture-side innovation. eSanjeevani is also being internationalised (interest from Fiji, the Philippines and Nigeria), reinforcing the ABDM/FHIR orientation as the durable national standard.

history.release_date: C-DAC's telemedicine technology 'Sanjeevani' dates from ~2002 (C-DAC tasked from 1999). eSanjeevani AB-HWC (provider-to-provider) launched November 2019; eSanjeevani OPD (patient-to-doctor) launched April 2020.
history.key_milestones: 1999 C-DAC tasked to develop indigenous telemedicine technology; ~2002 'Sanjeevani' released (store-and-forward plus real-time, tele-radiology/cardiology/pathology); Nov 2019 eSanjeevani AB-HWC launched; Apr 2020 eSanjeevani OPD launched; 2021 it crossed 1 crore consultations (Aug 2021) and ABDM launched (Sep 2021); 2022 eSanjeevani integrated with ABDM/ABHA (40+ apps integrated); Mar 2023 eSanjeevani 2.0 with PoCD device integration and AI; Apr 2023 CDSS integrated (structured capture + differential diagnosis); Sep 2023 deployed across all 28 states and 8 UTs with >160M consultations; Nov 2024 >276M; Apr 2025 National Awards for e-Governance context; 2025-2026 cumulative crossings from 43 crore to ~49 crore; Jul 2026 National e-Governance Gold Award (2026) for the AI CDSS; 2026 continued AI/multilingual roadmap and international interest.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: Within the last six months: 13 Feb 2026 PIB press note documented 282 million eSanjeevani consultations (Apr 2023-Nov 2025) benefiting from CDSS, with 12 million aided specifically by AI-recommended diagnoses. 17 Apr 2026 reporting put cumulative consultations above 463 million with 128,000+ in a single day, ~102 specialities, ~232,000 providers and ~18,600 hubs. 12 May 2026 coverage highlighted the CDSS's 300-symptom branching logic and 12 million AI-assisted consultations. 16 Jul 2026 the MoHFW received the National Award for e-Governance 2026 (Gold) for the AI CDSS integrated with eSanjeevani. 18 Jul 2026 the Defence Minister cited over 47 crore teleconsultations. 31 Jul 2026 Lok Sabha answers reported >48 crore patients (26 Jul), 1,41,171 spokes, 19,173 hubs, 890 online OPDs and ~2.39 lakh providers, and 48.95 crore cumulative with 2.13 crore AI differential diagnoses (30 Jul). 1 Sep 2026 reporting showed Karnataka as the largest eSanjeevani OPD user (54.1 lakh OPD consultations; ~3.1 crore total) and described introduced consultation-completeness rules (minimum two-minute consultations requiring history, allergies, diagnosis, investigations and prescription) plus per-consultation doctor incentives. Sep 2026 an Intelehealth policy brief (330M+ consultations) publicly criticised interoperability, connectivity and quality, and recommended FHIR/ABDM integration plus AI-based triage, multilingual history recording and structured follow-up. A Bhashini speech-to-speech translation pilot continues toward production.

market_positioning.target_users: Indian citizens/patients, particularly rural, remote and underserved populations, women and the elderly; frontline providers (Community Health Officers, ANMs, medical officers) at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs/PHCs; and hub doctors/specialists at medical colleges, CHCs and district hospitals, plus state/UT health administrations.
market_positioning.market_segment: National telemedicine / public digital-health infrastructure (remote consultation delivery plus interoperable EHR and e-prescription), sitting inside the Ayushman Bharat + ABDM ecosystem rather than in the AYUSH-software or ambient-scribing segments.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: eSanjeevani positions itself as India's National Telemedicine Service - a free, cloud-based system 'plugging the digital health divide' and the world's largest government-led telemedicine programme - offering doctor-to-doctor (AB-HWC) and patient-to-doctor (OPD) consultations, multilingual access, point-of-care diagnostics, AI-supported clinical decision support and ABHA-linked, interoperable health records that advance Universal Health Coverage.
